restatements.text: Requires cities to permit up to two homes on lots zoned for single-family use and prohibits cities from requiring a public hearing for these projects.

analysis.answer: Currently, cities determine the maximum number of homes permitted on residential lots and can mandate public hearings for project approvals. The measure changes this by requiring cities to allow up to two homes on single-family lots and banning public hearings for these specific projects.

Cities face minor administrative costs to update their zoning codes. Local governments face an opportunity cost by losing discretionary control over neighborhood density. Builders face lower compliance and holding costs due to the elimination of public hearings.

Property owners and developers benefit from expanded building rights and reduced procedural barriers. Future renters and buyers may benefit if housing supply increases. Existing residents who prefer lower density or wish to use public hearings to block development lose that ability and bear the cost of any localized impacts on parking or infrastructure.

Developers and property owners will likely apply to build duplexes or add second units on existing lots. Cities may respond by altering other zoning standards—such as height limits, parking requirements, or setbacks—to indirectly restrict such development or manage its impact without violating the specific text of the measure.

It addresses the problem of housing shortages and the spillover costs of exclusionary local zoning that restricts housing supply. The mechanism reaches this by preempting local density caps and removing discretionary public hearings. However, it may not result in widespread construction if other local rules (like setbacks, floor area ratios, or impact fees) remain restrictive.

The state government gains authority over local land-use policy. Property owners and developers gain discretion over how to use their residential lots. City councils, planning commissions, and neighborhood groups lose the power to veto or reshape these projects through the hearing process.

The effect of eliminating single-family zoning on housing supply and prices is debated. Some research finds that allowing duplexes increases overall housing supply and helps moderate regional prices. Other research suggests it can increase land values, lead to localized gentrification, or have limited impact on construction if other constraints (like setbacks or financial feasibility) remain.

Very little is lost in administration; the text establishes a clear prohibition on certain city actions, which builders can enforce through standard legal channels if a city attempts to mandate a hearing or deny a compliant project.
